blocks.text: Holding a cut slab of dark Pandoran rock in a gloved hand under a field lamp reveals something older than the moon, older than the star, and older than most of the elements in your own hand. The silicate rock, composed of oxygen, silicon, and magnesium, was fused in the shells of massive stars. The metallic glint comes from iron at the end of the fusion road, the fundamental reason this world has a core at all. The living light of carbon and nitrogen, shed by dying low-mass stars, now powers an entire biosphere. The truly interesting question is not just what this rock is. It is where every atom inside it has been.
Pick up a stone on Pandora.

It is not a remarkable one: there are no glowing seams, no veins of unobtanium, just a fist-sized piece of the crust from a riverbed somewhere in the Omatikaya forest. Turn it over in your hand. It is heavier than it looks, and darker. When you crack it open, the fresh face has a faint metallic glint in it, the way basalt does when there is iron in the melt.
Now ask the question nobody in the films ever asks: where did this come from?

I do not mean which volcano produced it, because that is a question about last week, geologically speaking. I mean the atoms themselves. Consider the iron creating that glint, the silicon and oxygen locked into the rock around it, the calcium, and the magnesium. Every single one of those nuclei had to be manufactured, individually, by a specific physical process, in a specific kind of place.

Those nuclei were then transported here across distances and timescales that make the four-light-year gap between Pandora and Earth look like a rounding error. The stone in your hand is the end of a supply chain that runs back thirteen billion years, and almost every link in that chain involves something dying.

The films open on a finished world: a breathable-looking sky, a vast forest, and a moon hanging gracefully beside a gas giant. This chapter asks what had to happen first. It turns out that reading the answer directly off Pandora's own stated properties leads somewhere the films very much did not intend.

sections.title: The universe had almost nothing to build with

blocks.text: Start at the beginning, because the beginning is unhelpfully empty.

For the first few minutes after the Big Bang, the whole universe was hot and dense enough to act as a cosmic fusion reactor, and for a while it behaved like one. Big Bang nucleosynthesis ran for roughly a quarter of an hour. Protons and neutrons found each other, deuterium formed as soon as the ambient light was too feeble to smash it apart again, and that deuterium fused into helium.
Then it stopped. It did not stop because the fuel ran out, since the universe is still three-quarters hydrogen today. It stopped because of an accident in the way atomic nuclei are built.

There is no stable nucleus with an atomic mass of five. There is no stable nucleus with an atomic mass of eight. Helium-four has an atomic mass of four. To get past it by the obvious route, you would add a proton or a neutron and land on mass five, which falls apart in under a sextillionth of a second.

If you add two helium nuclei together, you land on beryllium-eight, which lives for only about a hundred quintillionths of a second and then splits back into the two heliums it came from. Both obvious routes out of helium are completely closed.

There is only one way across: three helium nuclei colliding at essentially the same instant. That requires a density and temperature that the expanding universe blew past long before it could happen at scale.

So the cosmic ledger closes early, and it closes short. Hydrogen made up about seventy-five percent by mass. Helium made up about twenty-five percent. Deuterium, helium-three, and a whisper of lithium existed only as traces, in the parts-per-hundred-thousand range and below. And then nothing: no carbon, no oxygen, no silicon, no magnesium, no calcium, and no iron.

Consider the consequence, stated plainly: every atom in that stone except the hydrogen bound into its water was made after the Big Bang, inside a star. So was every atom in the tree you are standing under, and in your own hand. The universe did not come with rock. Rock is a manufactured product, and the factories are stars.

That is the foundational fact the rest of this chapter is built on, and it is worth sitting with for a moment, because it inverts the usual order of things. A world is not a place where matter happens to have gathered. It is a place where the residue of a long industrial history happens to have gathered, and that residue is specific enough to be read.
If stars made the elements, then different elements were made in different places, and the proportions in a given sample should be a record of which places contributed to it.
They are. And the record is stranger than saying a supernova did it.

Examining six samples from one moon reveals six different production histories. Note what happens to ocean water when you switch from weighing it to counting it: by mass it is overwhelmingly oxygen, which is supernova ash, but by atom it is two-thirds hydrogen, which predates every star that ever existed. Both readings are honest. They are answers to different questions.
Take the samples in order of increasing violence.

Ocean water is the one place a world still carries the first fifteen minutes of cosmic history. Weigh it and you get a supernova story, because oxygen is sixteen times heavier than hydrogen and dominates the scale. Count the atoms instead and two out of every three are primordial hydrogen, unchanged since before the first star lit. Every glass of water is mostly Big Bang.

A silicate mantle, which makes up the bulk of any rocky world, is almost entirely the work of massive stars that collapsed. Oxygen, magnesium, silicon, and calcium come out of the burning shells of stars above about eight solar masses. They are blown clear by a core-collapse supernova, and they come out fast, because such stars live only a few million years.

A metallic core shifts the story. Iron is the crossover element: roughly half of the galaxy's iron comes not from collapsing giants but from white dwarfs detonating in Type One-a supernovae. These happen hundreds of millions to billions of years later than core collapses do, because a white dwarf has to be made first and then has to wait. The iron in Pandora's core, and in the haemoglobin of everything walking on its surface, is mostly the ash of exploded stellar corpses.

A heavy-metal vein is where it gets genuinely extreme. Platinum, gold, thorium, and uranium are not made by standard stellar fusion at all. They require the rapid neutron-capture process: a flood of free neutrons so intense that atomic nuclei absorb them faster than they can decay. The only environments we have confirmed doing that are the collisions of neutron stars.

That last factory deserves a moment of attention, because we watched it happen. In August twenty seventeen, gravitational-wave detectors caught two neutron stars spiralling into each other. Telescopes turned to the resulting glow, and the spectrum of that glow carried the signatures of freshly minted heavy elements. It was the first direct observation of the process, and it settled an argument that had run for sixty years.

The only confirmed factory for gold, platinum, and uranium is two neutron stars colliding, throwing off a fraction of a solar mass of neutron-drenched debris. Two neutron stars touch for about one second of contact, and the heaviest elements are forged. A few percent of a solar mass is thrown clear as neutron-rich ejecta, seeded with gold, platinum, and uranium. That debris mixes outward for tens of millions of years before any of it can end up in rock. The elements in a heavy-metal vein were made in an event like this, long before Pandora's disk existed.

Consider how that historical argument was framed. The two neutron-capture routes were named for their tempo. The slow process runs inside puffed-up dying stars of modest mass, where neutrons trickle in over centuries and each nucleus has time to settle before the next arrives; it builds up to lead and stops. The rapid process runs in the shredded, neutron-drenched debris of a merger over about a second, and it runs so far past stability that it reaches uranium. Two processes, the same starting material, wildly different products: and a rock's mixture of them names which kind of catastrophe it inherited.

So the stone in your hand is not the ash of one event. It is a blend from at least four distinct classes of stellar death, spread over billions of years. Crucially, it required them in a particular order: the massive stars first to make oxygen and silicon, the white dwarfs later to top up the iron, and the neutron star mergers scattered throughout for anything heavier. A world assembled too early in cosmic history simply cannot be made of the right things.

sections.title: Which raises the question of when

blocks.text: Pandora's system has a real address, and that turns out to be a gift, because the fiction is silent on exactly the point the science can answer.

Canon never states how old Pandora is: not the moon, not Polyphemus, not the star system. There is no formation account anywhere in the official material. The world simply exists, finished, when the camera arrives.

But Alpha Centauri is not invented. It is the most closely measured star system in the sky after our own, and it has been weighed, aged, and chemically assayed by people with real instruments. Two numbers from that work matter here.

The first number is age. Asteroseismology, which reads the ringing modes of a star's interior the way you would read the timbre of a struck bell, puts Alpha Centauri A and B at about five point three billion years, give or take three hundred million. That is older than the Sun by roughly three-quarters of a billion years.

The second number is metallicity, and it is the more interesting of the two. Astronomers use the word to mean everything heavier than helium, which, from a rock's point of view, means everything a planet is made of. Both stars come in at about zero point two two dex above solar, which translates to roughly one point six times the Sun's supply of heavy elements.

That is not a minor footnote. Giant-planet occurrence scales steeply with host metallicity in the real exoplanet catalogue, for a mechanical reason: metals in the gas mean solids in the disk, and solids in the disk mean cores that can grow before the gas disperses. A system with one point six times the Sun's heavy elements is a system with a generous construction budget.

Looking at the measured numbers: Alpha Centauri has a measured system age of five point three billion years compared to our Sun at four point five seven billion years. Its abundance of heavy elements is one point six times the solar baseline. Meanwhile, official canon provides zero stated age for Pandora, Polyphemus, or the system.

So canon's gap gets filled from outside, and filled favourably. Pandora's system had more to build with than ours did, and more time to do it in. Both facts will matter shortly, and one of them will not be enough.
Before we can build a moon we should be honest about the machines that make its raw material, because the way a star works sets the pace of everything downstream.

A star is a slow-motion standoff. Gravity pulls every gram of it toward the centre; the pressure of hot gas pushes back. The standoff holds because the squeezing raises the core temperature until nuclei start fusing, and fusion releases the energy that maintains the pressure. Take the fusion away and the star falls in on itself; take the gravity away and it flies apart.

What is easy to miss is how narrowly this works. At ten million kelvin, two protons approaching each other still have roughly a thousand times too little energy to overcome their mutual electrical repulsion. Classically, nothing should happen at all. Fusion proceeds only because quantum mechanics allows a nucleus to occasionally appear on the far side of a barrier it cannot climb. Because a star contains so many protons, even an absurdly rare event happens often enough to keep it shining.
The consequence is a ferocious sensitivity to temperature, and the consequence of that is the thing that actually governs cosmic chemistry: heavy stars burn out fast.

Consider the extreme spread in stellar lifespans: a massive star of twenty-five solar masses burns through its hydrogen and collapses in about seven million years, before the disk of a young system would even disperse. A star of one solar mass lasts roughly ten billion years, remaining on the main sequence after the age of the galaxy's thin disk. Alpha Centauri B, at zero point nine solar masses, lasts about fifteen billion years, living longer than the universe is old.

Luminosity climbs as roughly the third-to-fourth power of mass, so a star twenty-five times the Sun's mass is a hundred thousand times brighter and spends its fuel a thousand times faster. Those are the stars that make the oxygen and silicon in Pandora's mantle, and they make it quickly, within a few million years of forming. Which is why the enrichment of the galaxy did not have to wait: the first generation of massive stars was already seeding its surroundings while the small stars born alongside them had barely begun.

The first stars had no metals to work with and nothing to cool their birth clouds, so they came out massive, and massive stars are impatient. They lit inside metal-free gas containing only hydrogen and helium, with no carbon, oxygen, dust, or rock to radiate heat away. Without coolants, collapsing clouds fragmented coarsely, making the first stars huge by default. They ignited, burned through everything, and detonated inside a few million years, which is why the universe stopped being a hydrogen desert so quickly.

Inside such a star the burning proceeds in stages, each hotter and faster than the last. The products stack into concentric shells like the rings of an onion: hydrogen fusing at the outside, then helium, then carbon, neon, oxygen, silicon, and at the very centre a growing ball of iron.
Two details in that sequence deserve naming, because both are load-bearing for the existence of anything at all.

The first is how carbon gets made. Three helium nuclei have to meet, which requires the fleeting beryllium-eight to survive just long enough for a third helium to arrive. It works only because carbon-twelve happens to have an excited state at almost exactly the energy the incoming pair brings with it: a resonance that boosts the triple-alpha process by about seven orders of magnitude. Without that coincidence there is no carbon, no oxygen made from carbon, and no chemistry worth discussing.

The second is why the sequence ends. Fusion releases energy only while it is climbing toward more tightly bound nuclei, and binding energy per nucleon peaks right around iron and nickel. Past that peak, fusing costs more than it yields. An iron core cannot pay for its own pressure. So the star's last act is a core that has no way left to hold itself up.

Every shell in a dying massive star is a different reaction running at a different temperature, and each one is shorter-lived than the last. The outermost hydrogen envelope lasts for millions of years. Moving inward, heavier shells of helium, carbon, neon, oxygen, and silicon burn progressively hotter and faster, with silicon fusion lasting only about a day. At the middle sits a dark iron core. Because fusing iron costs energy instead of releasing it, the furnace stops here, leaving the entire structure with only hours left before collapse.

When it collapses, the outcome is spectacular in a way the numbers understate. Over ninety-nine percent of the released energy leaves as neutrinos, which barely interact with anything; the mere one percent that stays behind is enough to unbind the entire outer star and fling it outward at thousands of kilometres per second. We know this is what happens because in nineteen eighty-seven a supernova went off close enough for underground detectors to catch a couple of dozen of those neutrinos, arriving hours before the light.

Enrichment and star formation are the same event seen twice. As the expanding shock front meets a cold, unenriched cloud of old gas waiting to be seeded, it compresses the gas past the point where it can hold itself up. The shell scatters newly made elements into the surrounding medium, and by triggering the collapse of that compressed gas, it turns the enriched material into the next generation of stars and their planets.

And then the crucial, easily skipped step: the debris has to mix. Ejecta plough into the surrounding interstellar medium, slow down, cool, and over tens of millions of years turbulently blend into the dense cold clouds where new stars form. Every generation of stars therefore begins slightly richer than the last, and a system forming five point three billion years ago around a star like Alpha Centauri A inherits the accumulated output of everything that died before it.
Which is where we can finally start building.

sections.title: A cloud that cannot help falling

blocks.text: Stars and their planets are made in the same event, out of the same material, and the event begins with a cloud deciding it is too heavy to stand up.

The cold molecular clouds where this happens are unimpressive by planetary standards: ten or twenty kelvin, thin enough that a laboratory would call them a hard vacuum. But they are enormous, and gravity cares about totals. There is a threshold, worked out in the nineteenth century, at which a clump's self-gravity beats the internal pressure resisting it: below a certain mass the clump just sits there, and above it the clump falls in. For a typical cold core the crossing point comes out around one or two solar masses, which is a satisfying thing to derive from scratch, because it is roughly the mass of a typical star.

Something usually has to nudge the cloud over the line. A passing shock from a nearby supernova will do it, which closes a pleasant loop, since the same event both enriches the gas and triggers the collapse that turns it into the next generation.
Then rotation intervenes, and this is the step that makes planets inevitable rather than optional.

Every cloud is turning a little. As it shrinks, conservation of angular momentum spins it faster, and material trying to fall straight in along the equator finds itself moving sideways too quickly to reach the centre. Gas falling in along the poles has no such problem. So the collapse is asymmetric: matter piles onto a central protostar from above and below, while everything near the equatorial plane settles into a spinning, flattened disk, a protoplanetary disk. It is not a chaotic cloud of debris, but something thin and orderly, with a temperature and a density that fall off smoothly outward.

Rotation is why planetary systems are flat. Most of the cloud's mass ends up in the newborn star, while almost all of its angular momentum does not. Gas with too much sideways motion to fall inward settles into a flat disk instead. Around Alpha Centauri A, that disk was not free to run outward forever. A companion star standing two dozen Earth-distances out gravitationally cut the disk short at about two point five to three astronomical units.

That last detail is specific to Pandora's system and worth flagging now, because it becomes a constraint later. Alpha Centauri B swings as close as about eleven Earth-distances from Alpha Centauri A. A companion that near does not merely light the sky; it gravitationally truncates the disk around its partner. Run the standard truncation estimates and the disk around Alpha Centauri A was cut off somewhere around two point five to three Earth-distances out.
Which is not much room to build in. Remember that.

sections.title: The disk sorts its own materials

blocks.text: A disk is not a bag of mixed ingredients. It is a sorting machine, and the sorting principle is temperature.

Gas near the star is hot; gas far out is cold; and every compound has a temperature below which it stops being a vapour and starts being a solid grain. So as you move outward, materials precipitate out of the gas in a strict order: the most refractory first, the most volatile last. Aluminium and calcium oxides condense while it is still well over a thousand kelvin. Silicates and metallic iron follow a few hundred degrees later. Sulfides and the alkali metals wait until it is a few hundred kelvin. Water ice needs to get down to about a hundred and seventy. Carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrogen are colder still, out where the disk is barely warmer than interstellar space.
The boundary where water freezes has a name and a disproportionate importance.

Following the condensation sequence outward illustrates how the available building material shifts. Inside the water line, only rock, metal, and sulfide have condensed, so anything built there comes out dense and dry. Cross the line and water ice joins the mix: the solid budget more than doubles, and the density of whatever assembles there falls by two-thirds. This one boundary decides whether a body is a rock or an iceball.

Water is abundant, so freezing it out roughly doubles the mass of solid material available for building. That is why giant planets form beyond the snow line and not inside it: only out there is there enough solid stuff to assemble a massive core quickly enough to matter.

It is also why the inner planets of any system come out dry. A body assembling inside the water line is made of rock and metal because rock and metal are the only things that have condensed there. Its water, if it ends up with any, has to be imported later.
Hold that thought too. It is about to collide with something.

sections.title: The gap in the middle of planet formation

blocks.text: Here is a problem that took thirty years to solve and is worth exploring because it is the most counter-intuitive step in the whole sequence.
Dust grains in a disk stick together when they touch gently, and grow: millimetre pebbles, centimetre clumps. But somewhere around the size of a fist to a metre, two things go wrong at once.
The first is that collisions stop being gentle. Turbulence stirs the disk, larger objects move faster relative to each other, and at those speeds a collision shatters or bounces rather than sticks.

The second is worse. The disk's gas is partly held up by its own pressure gradient, so it orbits slightly slower than a free-falling object would. A solid pebble feels no pressure support, orbits at full speed, and therefore experiences a permanent headwind. Drag bleeds off its orbital energy, and it spirals inward. For pebbles in the worst size range the spiral takes a few hundred years, which is nothing. Left alone, the disk's entire solid inventory drains into the star before anything large can form.

The way out is collective rather than individual. When enough pebbles accumulate in one region, they drag the local gas along with them, which reduces the headwind, which lets more pebbles accumulate in a runaway process. The pebbles pile into dense filaments through the streaming instability, and once a filament is dense enough its own gravity takes over and it collapses directly into bodies tens to hundreds of kilometres across. There is no gradual sticking through the forbidden sizes; the disk skips over them.

Planet formation has a gap in the middle. Objects between a fist and a metre across neither stick reliably nor survive their own inward drift, so growth cannot proceed one collision at a time. Loose grains in a pebble swarm drift inward faster the bigger they get. Under gas drag the swarm concentrates into dense filaments, and once self-gravity takes over, the clump collapses straight past the missing size range into full-sized planetesimals.

Once bodies that size exist, growth accelerates. In pebble accretion a planetesimal's gravity bends the paths of drifting pebbles toward it, so it sweeps a volume far larger than its own cross-section, and the biggest object in a neighbourhood grows fastest. Ten Earth masses of solid core in a few hundred thousand years is achievable, comfortably inside the two-to-five-million-year window before the gas disperses.

And a ten-Earth-mass core beyond the snow line is the trigger for something much larger. Its gravity begins holding onto the surrounding hydrogen and helium. The envelope it captures adds to the gravitational pull. Past a critical point the process runs away, hoovering up gas until the planet carves a gap in the disk and starves itself. That is how you get a gas giant.

Except that Polyphemus is not beyond the snow line. Canon puts it at about one Earth-distance from Alpha Centauri A: a Jupiter-class planet sitting in the temperate band, on ground where water never froze and the solid budget was thin.

So Polyphemus is an immigrant. A giant planet cannot assemble where canon parks it. There is not enough solid material inside the water line to build a ten-Earth-mass core before the gas is gone. What resolves this is not special pleading; it is the most ordinary process in modern planet formation, planetary migration. A planet exchanges angular momentum with the disk it sits in, and drifts. Hundreds of the real exoplanets we have found are giants far closer to their stars than they could possibly have formed, and migration is why. Polyphemus almost certainly built its core out past the water line, in the narrow band the companion star left available, and then moved inward to where the films find it. Canon does not say this. The physics does not really permit anything else.

Everything so far has been ordinary. Pandora's system is metal-rich, its disk was viable, and its giant planet took a well-travelled route. Now we come to the part that does not work, and it is worth being precise about why, because it is not a matter of taste.

A giant planet, in the act of accreting gas, spins up a miniature version of the disk that made it: a circumplanetary disk, fed from above by inflowing material, orbiting the planet rather than the star. Moons condense out of it. This is where the Galilean moons came from, and it explains their most obvious property: they orbit in the same direction, in nearly the same plane, on nearly circular paths, like a scale model of a solar system.

A giant planet builds its moons the way its star built it, in a flattened circumplanetary disk of its own, fed from above. A young giant is massive enough to open a gap in the stellar disk and keep feeding from its edges. This subdisk is the only thing feeding the moons, which is why satellite systems come out orderly and prograde. It is also why they come out small: each moon grows until it migrates inward and is eaten by the host, capping the total satellite system mass at about one ten-thousandth of the host planet.
It also imposes a limit, and the limit is startlingly consistent.

Three real satellite systems, with three very different hosts, follow one consistent ratio. Whatever a giant's mass, the moons it grows come to about a ten-thousandth of it. This is a self-limiting balance, because a moon growing heavier in a thin disk migrates inward faster and gets fed to the planet. Pandora sits an order of magnitude above that line, and dragging the host-mass slider does not rescue her: the mass Polyphemus would need is past where a planet stops being a planet.

Add up Jupiter's four Galilean moons and you get about two ten-thousandths of Jupiter. Saturn's whole satellite system, Titan included, comes to about one point five ten-thousandths of Saturn. Uranus's five major moons total about one ten-thousandth. Three systems, with hosts spanning a factor of twenty in mass, give the same answer to within a factor of two.

The mechanism behind that consistency is a negative feedback. A moon growing in the thin circumplanetary disk raises waves in it, and those waves push the moon inward, moving faster the heavier it gets. So the disk delivers its products to the planet about as fast as it makes them, and the standing inventory never exceeds a small fraction of the host.
Now put Pandora on that plot.

Canon gives Pandora a surface gravity of about zero point eight zero Earth gravities and a radius of about zero point seven five Earth radii. Those two numbers, with nothing else assumed, fix its mass at about zero point four five Earth masses. Against a Jupiter-mass Polyphemus, that is a ratio of roughly one point four thousandths, which is about fourteen times what a circumplanetary disk delivers.

You cannot fix this by making Polyphemus heavier. To bring a zero point four five Earth-mass moon inside the ceiling, you would need a host of about fourteen Jupiters, which is past the line where an object stops being a planet and starts fusing deuterium in its core. Nor can you fix it by shaving Pandora: the gravity and radius canon states are not negotiable without changing the world the films show.

Consider the meaning of this interesting failure. This is the best kind of problem a piece of world-building can have, because it is a quantitative one. Nothing about Pandora is impossible: the elements were available, the star is real and metal-rich, the disk was viable, and the giant's migration is routine. But an Earth-scale moon around a Jupiter-scale planet is not a thing a satellite system grows. It is a thing that has to be acquired some other way. And the same reasoning applies far beyond fiction: it is exactly why the search for real habitable exomoons is so daunting. The moons giant planets grow for themselves are Ganymedes and Titans, a hundredth of Earth's mass, not half of it. If large habitable moons exist, most of them are probably not native.
There are only three ways out, and we can weigh them against each other.

First, grow it in place anyway, with an exceptionally rich flow of solids into the circumplanetary disk. The system's high metallicity helps here, and the real literature does show that solid-driven torques can slow or reverse a moon's inward migration under the right conditions. This route keeps the tidy orbital architecture canon implies, where Pandora is one of fourteen moons, several of them large. But it is asking the mass ceiling to bend by an order of magnitude, and no observed system bends it that far.

Second, capture it. Pandora forms as an independent rocky planet in the temperate zone, and is taken prisoner as Polyphemus migrates inward through the same region. Neptune appears to have done exactly this to Triton. This route dissolves the mass problem entirely, because a captured world never had to grow inside anyone's disk. What it costs is orbital tidiness: capture normally leaves a steeply inclined, badly stretched orbit that needs a very long time to circularise, and it does nothing to explain Pandora's large siblings.

Third, build it from a collision. The circumplanetary disk grows several ordinary moons at the permitted scale, orbital resonances destabilise them during the migration, and two or three merge. Earth's Moon is the product of a collision of this general kind, in reverse. This route reaches the mass, keeps a prograde orbit, and has a bonus: the energy of such a merger would melt the resulting body throughout, which is convenient given what Pandora's density says about its interior.

Here is where I will leave it: canon supplies no formation account, so there is no fact here to be right or wrong about. What the physics does is rank the difficulties: the disk route strains a well-tested scaling law, capture strains the orbital architecture, and the merger route requires a specific violent accident at a specific time. My own reading is that the merger route asks least, because it needs luck rather than new physics. But that is an inference, and it should be read as one.

sections.title: What the density already told us

blocks.text: I have been treating Pandora's mass as an input. It is worth stopping to notice that it was never stated: it was derived, and the derivation says something about the interior that canon never claims and probably did not intend.

Surface gravity, radius, and mass: any two fix the third. Canon gives gravity and radius, so the mass follows, and once you have mass and radius you have mean density. Do the arithmetic and Pandora comes out at about five point nine grams per cubic centimetre. Earth is five point five one.

Comparing density values highlights the contrast: Pandora has a derived density of five point nine grams per cubic centimetre from the stated gravity and radius. Earth is five point five one, and Earth is more self-compressed than a smaller world would be. Ganymede, an ice moon, sits at one point nine four, Titan at one point eight eight, and Europa at three point zero one. That is the company Pandora is not keeping.

That number rules things out. An ice-and-rock moon of the kind giant planets actually grow, such as Ganymede, Callisto, or Titan, comes in under two grams per cubic centimetre, because it is roughly half water. Even Europa, the driest of the big icy moons, only reaches three. Pandora, at nearly six, is not in that family at all. It is denser than Earth despite being smaller, which means less self-compression working in its favour, which means the material itself must be heavier. Pandora is an iron-and-silicate world with a metallic core at least as large a fraction of it as Earth's core is of Earth.

Consider two moons of the same size, built on opposite sides of the water line. The pale, ice-rich moon was assembled beyond the water line: about half its mass is ice, so it comes out near two grams per cubic centimetre around a modest rocky centre. That is the kind of body a giant planet's disk actually produces. The dark, rock-and-metal moon was assembled inside the water line and differentiated into a large metal core under dense silicate. Pandora's stated gravity and radius give five point eight seven grams per cubic centimetre, picking the rock-and-metal body rather than the icy one. The difference is not decoration; it is a statement about where the material condensed.

Which is a second, independent argument that Pandora is not an ordinary moon. Its mass says a circumplanetary disk did not grow it. Its density says a circumplanetary disk could not have grown it: a disk out where Jupiter-class planets form is stocked with ice, and a body built there comes out light.

And this is where the vice closes, because there is a third thing to explain: Pandora has oceans and an atmosphere. Dense, dry, inner-disk material does not come with water. So the moon needs to be made of the sort of stuff that condenses close in, while carrying volatiles that only condense far out.

sections.title: Two problems the interior solves at once

blocks.text: The first half of that is not actually hard, because a freshly assembled world is molten, and molten worlds sort themselves.

The heat comes from several sources at once. Accretion itself plays a major role, as every falling body arrives at escape velocity and converts its motion to heat. Core formation adds more energy: as metal separates and sinks, its descent releases gravitational energy throughout the body. And radioactive decay played a vital part. This was not the slow uranium-and-thorium warmth that still drives Earth's interior today. It was a short-lived isotope of aluminium with a half-life under a million years, abundant enough in the early disk to melt anything forming within the first couple of million years.

The result is a magma ocean, and in a magma ocean elements distribute themselves by chemical preference. Some bind readily to oxygen and stay in the silicate melt; some dissolve into liquid metal and go down with it; some prefer sulfide; some refuse to stay in either and escape as gas. This is planetary differentiation, the sorting that gives every rocky world its layered structure. It is why Pandora's derived density implies not just heavy material but organised heavy material, with iron below and rock above.
It also creates a problem the chapter should name before leaving it, because it is the one place Pandora's cosmochemistry becomes genuinely unresolved.

Consider why an orebody is strange. Differentiation is very good at stripping metal-loving elements out of a crust. Platinum, gold, iridium, and their relatives, the siderophile elements, partition into liquid iron by factors of ten thousand or more. That is why Earth's crust is so poor in them relative to the bulk Earth: most of Earth's gold is in the core, unreachable. So a heavy, exotic phase concentrated in a crust at grades worth mining is not what differentiation produces by default. On Earth, ore deposits are the work of secondary processes: hydrothermal fluids, late magmatic sorting, or material delivered after the core had already finished forming. Unobtanium requires something of that kind. Canon offers no mechanism, and the physics of what the mineral does belongs to Floating Mountains, Unobtanium and the Superconductor. What belongs here is the plain statement that its concentration, not just its properties, is an unexplained problem.
The second half, the volatiles, turns out to be the part where we can be most confident, because the same forensic trick that solved it for Earth works for anywhere.

A tiny fraction of hydrogen atoms are deuterium: one proton, one neutron, twice the mass. Water made with deuterium behaves almost identically to ordinary water chemically, but the ratio between the two depends sharply on the temperature and chemistry of the environment where that water formed. Colder, more distant reservoirs end up deuterium-rich. And crucially, the ratio survives the trip: water delivered to a planet still carries the signature of where it came from.
So we can ask which reservoirs could have supplied an ocean, and check the answer against a measurement rather than a preference.

Seawater's isotope ratio is a constraint, not a curiosity. Carbonaceous asteroid water sits essentially on top of it. Comet sixty-seven P, measured directly by the Rosetta spacecraft, is more than three times heavier, so the arithmetic caps comets at a couple of percent of the delivery before the blend overshoots the ocean we actually have. Nebular gas fails from the other direction. The suppliers are not a matter of taste.

The nebular gas a planet forms in is far too light. Long-period comets are much too heavy. Comet sixty-seven P, measured up close by the Rosetta mission, came in at more than three times seawater's value. That result effectively removed comets as the main source of Earth's water, since even a modest cometary contribution would push the blend off the measured mark.

What matches, almost exactly, is the water bound into carbonaceous chondrites: dark, primitive asteroids from beyond the snow line, whose minerals hold water chemically rather than as ice. And in the last few years this stopped being an inference from meteorites that fell through the atmosphere and became a direct result, because two spacecraft went and collected samples. Hayabusa-two brought material back from the asteroid Ryugu; OSIRIS-REx brought back Bennu. Both are hydrated, both carry abundant organic matter, and both confirm the isotopic match.

So the delivery route is not mysterious. A world assembles dry inside the water line, and then icy and hydrated bodies from further out are scattered inward, most efficiently during exactly the kind of giant-planet migration Polyphemus has to have undergone. The same event that put Polyphemus in the temperate zone would have flung a great deal of wet material through it.

There is one thing in that air that does not fit. Canon's atmospheric inventory includes a slug of xenon at around five percent, an enormous figure for a heavy noble gas that on Earth is present at fractions of a part per million. Xenon is a genuine cosmochemical puzzle even here. Earth and Mars are both depleted in it relative to the meteorites they were built from. The leading explanation is that xenon was preferentially ionised and dragged away during early atmospheric escape. A world that kept five percent of it needs the opposite history: a gentle young star, an unusual delivery, or a crust that later gave xenon back. I raise it because a formation chapter should own it, and set it down because canon offers nothing to resolve it, and what that air does to a body belongs to What is in the Air.

A newly assembled world is hot enough to sort itself. Molten iron and nickel are denser than the silicate melt, so they sink, descending through the glowing interior and taking gold and platinum with them. At the centre, a dense core forms, occupying about a third of the body's radius, assembled in a few million years and still hot today. Meanwhile, gases dissolved in the melt escape through the crust: the first atmosphere is outgassed, not inherited. This is why Pandora's derived density implies not merely heavy material but organised heavy material, and why its air is a product of its interior rather than a leftover of its birth cloud.
So: turn the stone over one more time.

The hydrogen in the water clinging to it is primordial, thirteen and a half billion years old, unchanged since the first quarter-hour of everything. Its oxygen, silicon, and magnesium came out of massive stars that lived a few million years each and then blew themselves apart. Its iron is mostly the ash of white dwarfs that detonated, hundreds of millions of years later, once there had been time to make white dwarfs. If there is a thread of something heavier in it, that came from two neutron stars colliding, in about a second, somewhere in the galaxy, before the cloud that made this system had begun to fall in.

All of it was mixed into cold gas, compressed, and spun into a disk. It was sorted by temperature and gathered into pebbles that should have drifted into the star and did not. It assembled into a body that melted and sorted itself. Finally, it was rained on for a hundred million years by wet asteroids flung inward by a migrating giant.
That is not a poetic way of saying the stone is old. It is a supply chain, and every stage of it is a mechanism we can point at, most of them observed.

What the chapter cannot give you is the last link. Somewhere in that sequence, an Earth-scale rocky world ended up in orbit around a gas giant, and the ordinary route does not produce that. It was grown against the odds, or captured, or assembled from a collision. And the films, which never ask the question, also never close it.

Looking at the confidence meter for this chapter: sixty-five percent of this reconstruction is based on established real science, sixteen percent is direct astronomical inference, twelve percent comes from official canon, and seven percent is informed speculation.

Here is what stays open across five major questions. First: how old is Pandora? Canon never says, as there is no stated age for the moon, the planet, or the system anywhere in the official material. What we do have is real: asteroseismology puts Alpha Centauri A and B at about five point three billion years, roughly three-quarters of a billion years older than the Sun. Pandora cannot be older than its star, so that is a genuine ceiling, but nothing fixes where beneath it the moon actually sits. Second: where did an Earth-scale moon come from? This is unresolved, and not by a small margin. The satellite-to-host mass ratio observed across Jupiter, Saturn, and Uranus caps a disk-grown satellite system at about a ten-thousandth of its host; Pandora's derived mass is roughly fourteen times that. Growing it in place strains a well-tested scaling law, capture strains the orbital architecture canon implies, and a moon-moon merger requires a specific violent accident. Canon supplies no formation account to adjudicate between them. Third: why is unobtanium in the crust rather than the core? No official source explains it. Planetary differentiation strips dense metal-loving phases into the core with brutal efficiency, so an exotic heavy mineral concentrated at mineable grade in the shallow crust needs a secondary enrichment process, whether hydrothermal, late-magmatic, or delivered after core formation finished. Any of those is possible; none is stated. Fourth: where did five percent atmospheric xenon come from? Nobody has offered a mechanism, and it runs against the terrestrial pattern. Earth and Mars are both depleted in xenon relative to the meteorites they formed from, apparently because it was ionised and lost during early atmospheric escape. Retaining it in bulk would require an unusually quiet young star, an anomalous delivery of heavy noble gases, or prolonged release from crustal minerals. Fifth: did Polyphemus form where we find it? Almost certainly not, though canon does not address it. A Jupiter-class planet cannot assemble a core inside the water line, where solids are scarce, and the companion star truncated Alpha Centauri A's disk at only two or three Earth-distances, leaving a narrow band to build in. Formation beyond the snow line followed by inward migration is the ordinary explanation, and here it is close to a requirement.
Put the stone back where you found it. It has been through more than you have.
